Tidepools form in rocky depressions along the intertidal zone, where seawater is trapped as the tide recedes, creating a miniature and surprisingly stable ecosystem that must nonetheless withstand extreme swings in temperature, salinity, and oxygen levels over the course of a single day.

Organisms that thrive here, such as sea stars, hermit crabs, and anemones, have evolved specialized adaptations: thick mucus coatings to prevent desiccation, the ability to tolerate long stretches of direct sun exposure, and in some cases the capacity to regenerate lost limbs entirely after a predator attack.

Because tidepools are so accessible from shore, they are also among the most heavily studied marine habitats in introductory biology courses, offering students a hands-on way to observe predation, competition, and symbiosis without needing a boat, a wetsuit, or specialized diving equipment of any kind.
